title: A Time Capsule for 2276: What Would You Send to the Future?
summary: Imagine you could send a message to kids living 250 years from now. What would you put in a box to show them what life is like today? That's exactly what happened on July 4, 2026, when the United States turned 250 years old. To celebrate, officials buried a special time capsule in Philadelphia, right near where the Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776. But this isn't just any box. It's a super-tough steel container designed to survive underground for two and a half centuries. The engineer in charge, Michael Berilla, said, "Philadelphia would have to be six feet underwater for this time capsule to even possibly take on water." That's like saying it could survive a flood as deep as a tall person! Inside, every state and territory contributed something unique. Arkansas sent a real diamond. Maine added a bone from an endangered whale. Wisconsin included a feather from "Old Abe," a famous bald eagle that went into battle with soldiers during the Civil War. California went high-tech: they packed a computer chip and an AI-generated prediction of what the state might look like in 2276. Utah really went all out, sending 100 cards, 13 coins, documents, pins, and even two granite disks. The capsule will be marked by a cool sculpture shaped like a giant segmented snake. It's based on Benjamin Franklin's old cartoon "Join, or Die," which showed that the colonies needed to stick together to survive. The National Park Service also wrote down the exact location so future park rangers can find it. When the capsule is finally opened on July 4, 2276, the first thing people will see is a photo of the team who built it and a letter from Berilla. It says, "Greetings from the living, breathing hearts and hands of 2026. We will have long since returned to dust, but our devotion, pride, and unwavering hope for what our world could become are alive right here inside this steel. We built this for you." What would you put in a time capsule for the future?
why_it_matters: Thinking about what you would put in a time capsule helps you appreciate what's special about your own life right now and what you want kids in the future to know.

background_read: Time capsules are a way for people to send greetings and everyday objects to future generations. The oldest known time capsule in the United States was buried in 1795 by Paul Revere and Samuel Adams, two heroes of the American Revolution.

Benjamin Franklin (one of the most famous founding fathers) was a writer, inventor, and scientist. His cartoon ‘Join, or Die,’ showing a snake cut into pieces, urged the 13 original colonies to unite against a common enemy.

The National Park Service takes care of many historic places in the United States, including Independence Hall in Philadelphia where the Declaration of Independence was signed. Recording the capsule’s exact location helps future park rangers find it in 250 years.
Article_Structure: WHO: The United States, all 50 states and territories, engineer Michael Berilla, and the National Park Service.
WHAT: They created and buried a steel time capsule filled with items representing each state to be opened in 2276.
WHERE: In Philadelphia, on the grounds near where the Declaration of Independence was signed.
WHY: To celebrate America's 250th birthday and leave a lasting message from the people of 2026 to those living two and a half centuries later.

perspectives.description: Supporters say burying the capsule is a hopeful act that shows pride in today's country and faith that future people will still care about our story.
Some might argue the money and effort could have been used for solving current problems instead of sending objects to a very distant future no one can predict.
The items chosen show what different states find important now, but future historians might view them very differently, making the capsule a surprising history test.
